title: Swarming With Micro Air Vehicles: Fundamental Challenges, System Constraints, and Emerging Research Directions

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Micro Air Vehicle Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Definitions and Scope of MAV Swarms
subsections.content:
A micro air vehicle (MAV) swarm can be defined as a population of small flying robots that coordinate through local sensing, communication, or implicit interaction to produce system-level behavior that is robust, scalable, and not fully dependent on centralized supervision. In the aerial robotics literature, MAVs are typically distinguished from larger unmanned aerial vehicles by severe constraints on mass, payload, endurance, onboard computation, and sensing, which fundamentally shape feasible coordination strategies ref [1], ref [2]. Accordingly, a MAV swarm is not merely a group of co-located drones: it implies inter-agent coupling in decision-making, motion, or task execution, often inspired by distributed control and biological collectives ref [3], ref [4].

The scope of MAV swarming spans tightly coordinated formations, decentralized flocking, cooperative exploration, relay-based networking, and distributed perception. However, not every multi-UAV system qualifies as a swarm. Systems that rely on persistent global communication, centralized trajectory generation, or small team sizes with bespoke role assignment are better viewed as coordinated multi-robot systems rather than swarms in the strict sense ref [5], ref [6]. By contrast, swarm-oriented studies emphasize locality of interaction, online adaptability, redundancy, and graceful degradation under agent loss or uncertainty ref [4], ref [7].

This survey therefore uses MAV swarm to denote groups of physically embodied aerial robots—typically quadrotors or other lightweight flyers—whose collective behavior emerges from repeated agent-level rules under resource-constrained onboard operation. The definition includes both fully distributed implementations and hierarchical architectures that preserve local autonomy at execution time, but excludes purely simulated particle swarms and loosely coordinated fleets without meaningful collective coupling ref [2], ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Micro Air Vehicle Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Historical Evolution of Aerial Swarm Research
subsections.content:
Research on aerial swarming emerged from the broader study of collective motion and distributed coordination. Early theoretical foundations were established by Reynolds’ behavioral animation rules for flocking and by consensus-based formulations for coordinated control in networked multi-agent systems, which later became central to swarm guidance, formation keeping, and decentralized decision making in aerial robots ref [3], ref [5]. These ideas reframed coordinated flight as an interaction-topology problem rather than a purely centralized planning task.

A second phase translated such abstractions into robotic collectives through biologically inspired and self-organized systems. Surveys on swarm robotics consolidated principles such as local sensing, scalability, and robustness ref [10], while control-oriented work on flocking with obstacle avoidance provided practically relevant laws for mobile agents ref [11]. In parallel, vision-based demonstrations such as the FlyNUC platform showed that multiple indoor quadrotors could execute autonomous cooperative flight with onboard and external sensing pipelines, helping bridge swarm theory and MAV experimentation ref [12].

The modern MAV-swarm era was marked by reliable real-time state estimation, onboard computation, and communication-aware control. Distributed flight of large quadrotor teams was demonstrated in highly publicized experimental studies on cooperative trajectory generation and formation transitions ref [13], and later extended toward communication-constrained and outdoor autonomous swarms ref [14], ref [15]. Recent work has further emphasized fully decentralized planning, reciprocal collision avoidance, and onboard perception, enabling denser and more resilient MAV collectives in cluttered environments ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Micro Air Vehicle Swarming
subsections.content:
Application scenarios for MAV swarms are shaped by the combination of limited onboard resources, close-range sensing, and the ability to distribute coverage and risk. A recurring mission profile is cooperative exploration and mapping in GPS-denied or cluttered environments, where multiple vehicles jointly localize, build maps, and maintain sufficient spacing to enlarge the sensed volume beyond what a single MAV can achieve. Early demonstrations of decentralized multi-UAV flight and sensing already highlighted surveillance, patrol, and area coverage as motivating use cases ref [18], while later works on autonomous flight of drone swarms in forests and other dense environments showed the relevance of distributed navigation for search and reconnaissance missions ref [19].

A second major class comprises disaster response and inspection. In these missions, swarms are valued for rapid situational awareness, persistent observation from multiple viewpoints, and graceful degradation under individual failures. Multi-robot search-and-rescue has long framed heterogeneous and cooperative aerial teams as a way to speed victim search and environmental assessment ref [20]. More recent systems have demonstrated collaborative visual–inertial navigation, target tracking, and formation flight outdoors, supporting mission profiles such as perimeter monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and dynamic target following ref [21], ref [22]. Distributed collision avoidance and reciprocal sensing are especially important when these tasks must be executed in tight airspace or with intermittent communication ref [16].

At the smallest scales, mission design is also constrained by payload and endurance, which favors short-horizon tasks such as source seeking, plume tracking, and localized environmental monitoring. Bio-inspired swarms of miniature flying robots have been proposed for distributed sensing under severe size and energy constraints ref [23], and collective transport or cooperative manipulation has emerged as a specialized mission profile when individual MAVs cannot carry the required payload alone ref [24]. More broadly, vision papers on swarms emphasize the transition from isolated demonstrations to application-driven deployments in monitoring, cinematography, and warehouse-like logistics, where the central challenge is to translate high-level coverage or service goals into safe, decentralized behaviors ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Micro Air Vehicle Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Swarm Design Objectives and Performance Criteria
subsections.content:
Swarm design objectives for micro air vehicles are inherently multi-objective: the swarm should achieve mission-level effectiveness while preserving decentralization, safety, and feasibility on severely resource-constrained platforms. In practice, common objectives include scalability with team size, robustness to agent loss and communication degradation, adaptability to dynamic environments, and low per-agent sensing, computation, and communication requirements. These criteria are central to distributed flocking and consensus formulations, where stability and cohesion must emerge from local interactions rather than centralized coordination ref [11], ref [5], ref [26].

Mission performance is usually evaluated through task-dependent metrics such as area coverage, target localization success, tracking continuity, mapping completeness, and completion time, while swarm-quality metrics emphasize cohesion, connectivity, collision avoidance, and resilience under failures. For MAVs, these metrics must be balanced against flight-endurance limits and aggressive dynamic constraints; hence energy efficiency, communication load, and onboard estimability become first-class performance criteria rather than secondary implementation details ref [27], ref [28], ref [21].

A distinctive concern in MAV swarms is the tight coupling between control objectives and embedded autonomy. Vision- or relative-localization-based teams must maintain formations that are not only geometrically useful but also observable and collision-safe, and they must do so under uncertain state estimation and asynchronous communication. Consequently, recent work often evaluates systems end-to-end, combining task success with formal or empirical measures of safety, distributed executability, and real-time onboard operation in large collectives ref [29], ref [30], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Micro Air Vehicle Swarming
subsections.subsection_title: Comparison With Ground and Larger Aerial Swarms
subsections.content:
MAV swarms inherit many ideas from ground multi-robot systems, but the operating envelope is fundamentally different. Relative to wheeled swarms, MAVs must continuously generate lift, stabilize under fast nonlinear dynamics, and coordinate under tight mass, power, and computation limits. Ground swarms often exploit persistent contact, accurate odometry, and structured environments, enabling distributed coverage, formation, and task-allocation methods that are harder to transfer directly to aerial platforms ref [31], ref [32]. In contrast, MAV teams face stronger coupling between control and communication, reduced endurance, and greater sensitivity to wind and localization dropouts, which makes decentralized flocking and collision avoidance more tightly constrained in time and space ref [11], ref [33].

Compared with larger aerial swarms, MAV swarms trade payload, sensing range, and onboard processing for deployability, safety, and operation in cluttered indoor or near-structure environments. Large-UAV coordination has emphasized wide-area networking, long-range deconfliction, and airspace-level planning ref [34], ref [5], whereas MAV swarms often rely on short-range relative sensing and local interaction rules derived from biological flocking and distributed robotics ref [35], ref [36]. The small scale of MAVs also changes failure modes: aerodynamic interactions, actuator saturation, and downwash become dominant at close spacing, while GPS-denied flight and onboard perception constraints are routine rather than exceptional ref [33], ref [37].

These differences imply that evaluation criteria are not directly interchangeable across domains. Ground swarms may prioritize throughput, coverage, or warehouse-style efficiency, and larger aerial swarms may optimize persistence or theater-scale coordination; MAV swarms instead emphasize agility, safe density, resilience to partial observability, and mission completion under severe energy budgets. Accordingly, the field has converged on lightweight distributed architectures and experimentally validated local behaviors rather than the heavier sensing, communication, and planning stacks common in larger UAV systems ref [11], ref [5], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Platform-Level Constraints and System Architecture
subsections.content:
Size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints are among the most fundamental determinants of MAV swarm capability because they couple airframe scale to endurance, payload capacity, sensing range, and communication hardware. Early analyses of centimeter-to-decimeter vehicles showed that miniaturization does not simply reduce performance proportionally; Reynolds-number effects, reduced actuator authority, and unfavorable battery mass fractions can sharply compress the feasible operating envelope relative to larger UAVs [1], [2]. These limits are especially consequential in swarms, where each vehicle must reserve mass and energy not only for flight but also for inter-robot localization, communication, and fail-safe autonomy.

At the platform level, the dominant bottleneck is usually stored energy. Practical quadrotor and nano-air-vehicle designs consistently exhibit short flight times because propulsion power scales unfavorably with aggressive maneuvering and with added sensing or compute payloads [3], [4]. The resulting trade-off is architectural: adding cameras, range sensors, shielding, or larger batteries can improve autonomy and robustness, but often at the cost of reduced agility and shorter mission duration per unit mass [5], [6]. For swarm deployment, this means that algorithmic assumptions about persistent sensing, dense communication, or onboard mapping must be reconciled with highly constrained per-vehicle energy budgets.

SWaP limitations also shape collective design choices. Lightweight platforms often offload perception or planning to motion-capture systems, external infrastructure, or edge computers, as seen in early large-scale flight demonstrations [7], whereas more autonomous micro-aerial systems require carefully co-designed hardware and software stacks to stay within mass and power budgets [8], [9]. Bio-inspired and insect-scale vehicles further illustrate the extreme end of this spectrum: at milligram to gram scales, available payload and onboard energy become so limited that even basic sensing and control must be radically simplified [10]. Consequently, SWaP is not merely a vehicle-level specification; it defines the boundary conditions for scalable swarm autonomy.

subsections.section_title: Platform-Level Constraints and System Architecture
subsections.content:
Flight dynamics impose hard limits on what MAV swarms can reliably execute. Quadrotors are underactuated, strongly coupled, and bandwidth-limited systems whose translational motion is achieved only through attitude changes, creating delays between collective planning commands and realizable accelerations. Aggressive maneuvers therefore trade tracking accuracy for stability margin, especially on lightweight platforms with flexible frames, motor saturation, and limited thrust-to-weight ratio. These effects are evident in nonlinear modeling and control studies for quadrotors and in high-speed trajectory tracking work that exposes the gap between differential-flatness-based planning and actuator-feasible execution [1,2,3].

Control limitations are amplified in swarms because disturbance rejection, estimation error, and communication delay propagate into inter-robot coordination. Classical cascade PID architectures remain attractive for embedded simplicity, but they degrade under aerodynamic uncertainty and rapid setpoint changes, motivating model-based and geometric controllers with stronger guarantees on SE(3) [4,5]. Even then, safe relative flight is constrained by downwash, wake interactions, and the need to preserve attitude authority during close formation, which narrows feasible spacing and vertical stacking in dense teams [6,7].

At the collective level, these dynamics require planners to respect bounded acceleration, jerk, and stopping distance rather than treating agents as ideal single integrators. Minimum-snap trajectory generation and onboard replanning methods explicitly encode dynamic feasibility, while recent swarm demonstrations show that performance scales only when coordination laws are co-designed with vehicle-level control and sensing limits [2,8,9]. Thus, flight-control constraints are not merely implementation details; they fundamentally shape achievable swarm geometry, responsiveness, and robustness in real deployments [10].

subsections.section_title: Platform-Level Constraints and System Architecture
subsections.content:
Onboard sensing is a primary bottleneck for MAV swarms because payload, power, and field-of-view constraints limit both state estimation quality and the richness of inter-robot perception. Vision-based sensing is attractive due to low mass and information density, but monocular systems suffer from scale ambiguity and sensitivity to texture, lighting, and motion blur, while stereo and RGB-D increase mass, power draw, and computational demand. These trade-offs are evident in widely used visual-inertial pipelines such as PTAM, ORB-SLAM, and VINS-Mono, and in lightweight stereo systems for obstacle avoidance and onboard mapping ref [58], ref [59], ref [60], ref [61], ref [62].

In practice, MAVs therefore rely on tightly coupled sensor fusion, typically combining IMUs with cameras, range sensors, and occasionally GPS or motion-capture priors. Visual-inertial odometry improves drift and robustness relative to vision alone, but aggressive maneuvers still create estimator degradation through vibration, rolling-shutter effects, and temporary feature loss. Event cameras offer a promising alternative under high-speed motion and high dynamic range, enabling low-latency perception on resource-constrained platforms, though they introduce different algorithmic and calibration burdens ref [60], ref [63], ref [64].

For swarms, sensing limitations are amplified by mutual occlusion, restricted relative observability, and the difficulty of maintaining reliable inter-agent ranging or identification without dedicated infrastructure. UWB can provide lightweight relative localization support, but accuracy degrades under non-line-of-sight conditions and multipath, and integration with onboard estimators remains nontrivial. As a result, collective autonomy often depends on simplified sensing assumptions, sparse communication of state estimates, or external aids rather than fully onboard perception of all neighbors ref [65], ref [66], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Platform-Level Constraints and System Architecture
subsections.content:
Embedded computation is a primary bottleneck in MAV swarms because flight stabilization, state estimation, sensing, communication, and coordination must all execute under strict latency and power budgets on lightweight processors. Early onboard autonomy demonstrations already showed that estimator-control loops, visual processing, and communication scheduling compete for scarce CPU and memory resources, forcing tightly integrated software architectures and careful task prioritization ref [67], ref [68]. Consequently, many swarm systems adopt hierarchical designs in which fast inner-loop control remains fully onboard while computationally heavier mapping, planning, or global coordination is simplified, event-triggered, or partially offloaded ref [69].

Real-time perception is especially demanding. Vision-based odometry and obstacle avoidance have been made feasible on pocket-sized platforms, but only through aggressive algorithmic efficiency, low-resolution sensing, and hardware-conscious implementations ref [70], ref [71]. Similarly, event-based and lightweight visual-inertial pipelines reduce latency and bandwidth relative to frame-based processing, improving responsiveness in high-speed flight while preserving onboard deployability ref [63], ref [64]. These design choices directly affect swarm behavior: limited onboard inference often favors local reactive rules, sparse communication, and decentralized estimation over globally optimal but computationally intensive strategies.

At the systems level, embedded middleware and scheduling strongly influence robustness. PX4-class autopilot stacks and ROS-compatible aerial software frameworks have accelerated modular development, yet they also expose trade-offs between abstraction, determinism, and resource overhead ref [72], ref [73]. More broadly, surveys of onboard computer vision for drones emphasize that energy-aware co-design of algorithms, processors, and sensing is essential if dense perception and learned policies are to scale from single MAVs to multi-robot swarms ref [74].

subsections.section_title: Platform-Level Constraints and System Architecture
subsections.content:
Mechanical design fixes much of the feasible swarm operating envelope because airframe geometry, propulsion layout, and structural choices jointly determine thrust margin, agility, endurance, and robustness. Standard quadrotors remain dominant because their symmetric layout simplifies control allocation and packaging, but this simplicity trades away actuator redundancy and fault tolerance. Hexa- and octorotor configurations improve payload capacity and graceful degradation under rotor loss at the cost of mass, drag, and reduced energy efficiency per unit payload, while coaxial arrangements increase compactness but introduce aerodynamic interference and control-coupling penalties ref [73], ref [49], ref [75]. For dense swarms, these platform-level differences matter collectively: larger downwash footprints, higher acoustic signatures, and wider rotor disks constrain inter-vehicle spacing and safe formation geometry.

Propulsion selection is equally consequential. Rotor diameter, disk loading, and motor–propeller matching determine hover efficiency and transient authority: larger propellers reduce induced power but enlarge the vehicle and increase susceptibility to blade interference in compact formations, whereas smaller high-speed rotors favor maneuverability and compactness but shorten endurance and amplify sensitivity to manufacturing tolerances ref [76], ref [77]. At small scales, Reynolds-number effects and low-inertia actuation degrade propeller efficiency, helping explain the sharp performance gap between centimeter-scale vehicles and larger MAVs; this has motivated alternative actuation concepts inspired by insects, though these introduce demanding transmission, fabrication, and control challenges ref [47], ref [78].

Mechanical robustness also trades against mass budget. Protective frames and ducts can improve collision tolerance and enable operation near obstacles or humans, but often incur drag, added inertia, and complex flow interactions that offset nominal safety benefits ref [79], ref [80]. More broadly, morphology-aware co-design—where body structure, propulsors, and control are optimized together—has emerged as a key direction for swarm-capable platforms because small per-vehicle improvements in efficiency or resilience can scale into large gains in mission duration, deployment density, and maintenance burden ref [81].

subsections.section_title: Collective Perception, Communication, and Coordination Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Inter-agent communication models in MAV swarms are typically designed around severe payload, power, and spectrum constraints, which favor decentralized exchange of low-rate state summaries over centralized streaming architectures. Early distributed control results formalized how local communication graphs shape collective behavior, showing that consensus and formation objectives can be achieved when each vehicle exchanges only neighbor information under suitable connectivity conditions ref [5], ref [82]. This graph-based view remains foundational because it abstracts heterogeneous radio links, intermittent packet loss, and time-varying neighborhoods into analyzable communication constraints.

A major distinction is between explicit communication, in which MAVs transmit messages over wireless links, and implicit communication, in which motion itself encodes intent or state. In practice, explicit broadcast or gossip-style models dominate for relative state sharing, task allocation, and map fusion, whereas biologically inspired swarm systems often minimize message content to simple local cues or even communication-free interaction rules ref [11], ref [83]. For larger collectives, scalable communication models increasingly rely on event-triggered updates, compressed state exchange, and asynchronous protocols to reduce bandwidth while preserving stability and agreement guarantees ref [84], ref [85].

The communication model is also tightly coupled to the physical networking stack. Studies of robotic and UAV networks emphasize that medium-access contention, delay, and finite throughput can materially alter closed-loop performance, motivating cross-layer co-design between control and networking ref [86], ref [87]. More recent swarm-oriented architectures therefore combine local peer-to-peer exchange with adaptive routing or software-defined coordination layers, enabling resilience to topology changes and partial failures in dense aerial teams ref [88].

Overall, the literature converges on a view of communication as a scarce shared resource: the most effective models are not those that maximize information flow, but those that expose just enough structured neighbor information to sustain estimation, safety, and coordinated action under dynamic connectivity.

subsections.section_title: Collective Perception, Communication, and Coordination Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Network Topology, Connectivity, and Bandwidth Management
subsections.content:
Network topology strongly shapes the stability and scalability of multi-MAV cooperation because information flow, robustness to failures, and convergence rates all depend on graph structure. Early consensus results established that agreement can be achieved under dynamically changing interaction graphs provided appropriate joint connectivity conditions hold, giving a theoretical basis for time-varying aerial networks ref [5], ref [89]. In practice, algebraic connectivity has become a central design metric because it links topology to estimation quality, controllability, and resilience; this motivates connectivity-aware motion planning and formation maintenance strategies that explicitly regulate graph spectra during flight ref [90], ref [91].

For MAV swarms, connectivity maintenance is complicated by mobility, occlusion, and limited sensing range. Decentralized controllers that preserve communication links while allowing task-directed motion were developed in the multi-robot literature and remain highly relevant to aerial teams ref [92]. For flying ad hoc networks, topology control must also account for highly dynamic channels and intermittent packet loss, leading to cross-layer designs that jointly reason about routing, mobility, and link quality ref [93]. Connectivity is therefore rarely treated as a hard binary property alone; instead, practical systems often seek graceful degradation, preserving a connected backbone or k-neighbor structure sufficient for coordination and shared situational awareness.

Bandwidth management further constrains topology design because all-to-all exchange is rarely sustainable as team size grows. Event-triggered and self-triggered communication reduce traffic by transmitting only when local state innovation is significant, while still retaining consensus or formation guarantees under suitable conditions ref [94], ref [95]. Relatedly, gossip-based and broadcast-efficient coordination schemes trade convergence speed for lower channel occupancy and improved scalability ref [96]. In perception-heavy missions, adaptive communication policies that prioritize informative measurements or compressed map updates are especially important, echoing broader networked control results on stabilization under finite data rates ref [97].

subsections.section_title: Collective Perception, Communication, and Coordination Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Relative Localization and Shared State Estimation
subsections.content:
Relative localization and shared state estimation are foundational for MAV teams because fully independent global positioning is often unavailable, inaccurate, or inconsistent across agents. Early work showed that cooperative localization can reduce drift by fusing inter-agent range or bearing constraints with onboard inertial and exteroceptive sensing, provided that cross-correlations are handled consistently in decentralized filters ref [98], ref [99]. In MAV settings, this problem is especially acute because fast motion, limited payload, and intermittent communication make centralized estimation fragile, motivating estimation architectures that retain local autonomy while exploiting relative observations.

A major line of research uses vision, ultra-wideband ranging, or motion-capture-free relative sensing to estimate pairwise pose and velocity. Vision-based relative navigation has been demonstrated for aerial robots using onboard cameras and visual markers or natural features, enabling leader-follower flight and mutual pose recovery without external infrastructure ref [100], ref [101]. Complementary UWB-inertial fusion provides lightweight range-based localization in cluttered or GPS-denied environments, and has been integrated with optimization or filtering pipelines for multi-robot state estimation ref [102], ref [103]. Such systems trade observability, update rate, and robustness to occlusion against communication load and calibration complexity.

Shared state estimation further requires consistency across the network under delayed, lossy communication. Distributed smoothing and factor-graph formulations have become influential because they separate local sensing from sparse inter-robot constraints and allow scalable map and trajectory fusion ref [104], ref [105]. For resource-constrained teams, covariance intersection and related conservative fusion rules remain important when unknown correlations arise from information reuse ref [106]. More recent decentralized visual-inertial and multi-robot SLAM systems show that accurate shared state can be maintained through selective exchange of keyframes, loop closures, or condensed belief representations rather than raw sensor streams ref [105], ref [107].

subsections.section_title: Collective Perception, Communication, and Coordination Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Consensus, Flocking, and Distributed Coordination Laws
subsections.content:
Consensus and flocking laws provide a compact abstraction for distributed MAV coordination: each vehicle updates its state from local neighbor information to achieve agreement on headings, velocities, task variables, or geometric formations. Early graph-theoretic analyses established that convergence depends on connectivity and interaction weights, including under dynamically changing neighbor sets ref [5], ref [89]. For MAVs, these results motivate decentralized controllers that avoid single points of failure and naturally match short-range sensing and communication constraints.

Flocking formulations typically combine separation, velocity alignment, and cohesion terms. Reynolds’ behavioral rules remain influential as an algorithmic template ref [3], while control-theoretic refinements introduced provable stability and collision avoidance for dynamic agents. In particular, Olfati-Saber’s free-space flocking framework linked collective motion to artificial potentials and consensus-like coupling ref [11], and the Vicsek model provided a minimal stochastic perspective on emergent alignment under local interactions ref [108]. Extensions to nonholonomic vehicles and rigid-body formations further connected flocking to formation stabilization and graph rigidity concepts relevant to quadrotor teams ref [109], ref [110].

Recent MAV work emphasizes distributed coordination under uncertainty, asynchronous updates, and obstacle-rich environments. Distributed MPC offers a systematic way to enforce dynamic and safety constraints while preserving local decision making ref [111]. In parallel, broadcast and event-triggered consensus schemes reduce communication load without fully sacrificing convergence guarantees, an important property for bandwidth-limited aerial swarms ref [112]. Collectively, these approaches illustrate the trade-off between analytic simplicity of consensus laws and the richer constraint handling required for reliable real-world multi-MAV deployment ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Collective Perception, Communication, and Coordination Mechanisms
subsections.content:
Collective perception seeks to overcome the limited field of view, occlusion sensitivity, and range constraints of individual MAVs by fusing spatially distributed observations into a shared environmental representation. In swarm settings, this typically combines local visual or range sensing with decentralized map exchange, allowing the team to infer object extent, free space, and task-relevant semantics that are not observable from any single viewpoint. Early multi-robot mapping work established the benefits of distributed occupancy-grid fusion and cooperative exploration for extending situational awareness under partial observability [1], [2].

For MAVs, the problem is complicated by fast ego-motion, intermittent communication, and payload-limited sensing. Collaborative visual SLAM and multi-view reconstruction methods therefore emphasize compact map representations, inter-robot loop closures, and delayed-consistent fusion rather than raw data sharing. Systems such as C-SLAM and collaborative visual inertial pipelines demonstrate that pose-graph exchange can support large-scale shared mapping with bounded bandwidth [3], [4], while distributed dense mapping and online 3D reconstruction show how teams can jointly recover geometry from complementary viewpoints [5], [6].

Beyond geometry, recent work has moved toward semantic and task-level environment understanding. Distributed semantic mapping enables robots to share object- or class-level beliefs instead of only metric structure, improving search, inspection, and interaction planning [7], [8]. In parallel, active perception and next-best-view strategies coordinate sensing actions so that the swarm not only communicates observations, but also reconfigures itself to maximize information gain over poorly observed regions or targets [2], [9], [10]. Overall, collective perception is most effective when estimation, communication, and motion planning are co-designed around uncertainty, redundancy, and the value of information.

subsections.section_title: Swarm Control, Planning, and Autonomy
subsections.content:
Decentralized and distributed control architectures are central to MAV swarms because they avoid single points of failure, reduce communication bottlenecks, and permit scalability under limited onboard computation. Early consensus-based formulations established how local neighbor interactions can yield globally coherent motion and agreement, providing a mathematical basis for distributed coordination under switching communication graphs and sparse information exchange [1], ref [89]. For aerial swarms, these ideas are typically instantiated through graph-based feedback laws in which each vehicle regulates relative position, velocity, or heading using only nearby measurements, rather than relying on a central planner.

A major line of work casts swarm coordination as cooperative control over networked dynamical systems. Surveys by Olfati-Saber et al. and Ren et al. synthesized leader-follower, consensus, and containment strategies that remain influential for MAV teams operating with time-varying connectivity and communication delays [3], ref [122]. Distributed model predictive control further extends this paradigm by explicitly handling constraints and collision envelopes while preserving local autonomy; Richards and How demonstrated decentralized receding-horizon coordination for multiple vehicles, and Dunbar and Murray analyzed distributed MPC schemes for stabilizing formations with partial information [5], ref [124].

In practice, MAV implementations often combine high-rate local feedback with lower-rate inter-agent synchronization. The ETH Zurich multi-quadrotor testbeds highlighted how onboard state estimation, relative localization, and distributed trajectory generation can support robust multi-agent flight without full centralization [7], ref [126]. More recent platform-oriented work has emphasized modular distributed autonomy stacks that separate estimation, planning, and coordination while retaining resilience to packet loss and asynchronous updates [9]. Overall, effective architectures balance theoretical guarantees with pragmatic issues including sensing range, latency, heterogeneity, and graceful degradation when communication becomes intermittent.

subsections.section_title: Swarm Control, Planning, and Autonomy
subsections.content:
Formation control in MAV swarms seeks to preserve prescribed inter-agent geometry while remaining scalable, communication-efficient, and robust to sensing uncertainty. A major line of work models the swarm as a graph and stabilizes formations through distance- or displacement-based feedback. Rigidity theory provides the key observability and uniqueness conditions for distance-constrained shapes, showing when local relative measurements are sufficient to recover and maintain a global formation up to trivial motions ref [127], ref [110]. Gradient laws on inter-agent distances offer simple decentralized controllers, but they can admit reflected or otherwise incorrect equilibria; this motivated almost-global and infinitesimal-rigidity-based designs that strengthen convergence guarantees for minimally sensed teams ref [128], ref [26].

For aerial robots, shape maintenance must be integrated with dynamic feasibility and trajectory generation. Consensus and virtual-structure formulations have therefore been extended to quadrotor formations with onboard position feedback and distributed estimation, enabling coordinated translation, scaling, and maneuvering under nonholonomic and actuation constraints ref [5], ref [49]. Bearing-only and stress-matrix approaches further reduce sensing demands and permit similarity transformations such as formation resizing, which is valuable for obstacle negotiation and camera-footprint adaptation ref [129], ref [130]. In practice, these controllers are often layered with model predictive or differential-flatness-based planners so that nominal shape objectives coexist with thrust limits and collision constraints.

Recent MAV demonstrations emphasize resilience: maintaining shape despite packet drops, switching interaction graphs, and the loss or addition of agents. Distributed receding-horizon controllers and continuum-deformation methods support reconfiguration while preserving safety margins, whereas flight-tested outdoor systems illustrate that accurate relative localization and delay-aware coordination remain the main bottlenecks to reliable long-duration shape maintenance ref [131], ref [132]. Overall, the literature shows a progression from static graph-theoretic guarantees toward dynamically feasible, reconfigurable formations suitable for real-world swarm autonomy.

subsections.section_title: Swarm Control, Planning, and Autonomy
subsections.content:
Collision avoidance in MAV swarms must couple fast local reaction with guarantees on inter-agent separation, obstacle clearance, and mission continuity under sensing and communication uncertainty. Early reciprocal-avoidance methods such as ORCA provided a computationally efficient distributed mechanism for collision-free multi-agent motion by projecting locally feasible velocities under mutual responsibility assumptions ref [133]. For aerial vehicles, velocity-obstacle formulations were extended to dynamic environments and integrated with onboard sensing, enabling real-time avoidance without centralized trajectory recomputation ref [134].

Recent safety-critical navigation frameworks increasingly combine planning and control through formal constraint enforcement. Control barrier functions offer forward-invariance guarantees for safety sets and have been integrated with quadratic-program-based controllers for collision avoidance in nonlinear systems ref [135], while predictive control supplies finite-horizon handling of dynamics, actuator limits, and multi-agent coupling ref [136]. In quadrotor teams, decentralized model predictive control has been shown to support collision-free trajectory generation in cluttered spaces with only local information or shared intent ref [137], and differential-flatness-based planning further enables dynamically feasible evasive maneuvers at high speed ref [49].

For dense swarms, the main challenge is preserving scalability without sacrificing certificates of safety. Safe corridor generation and convex decomposition reduce the complexity of multi-robot planning in obstacle-rich scenes ref [138], whereas robust and chance-constrained formulations explicitly address state-estimation error and disturbances ref [139]. Learning-based perception and policy adaptation can improve responsiveness in unknown environments, but current survey evidence suggests they are most reliable when wrapped by model-based safety filters or reachability-style backup controllers rather than used as standalone collision-avoidance mechanisms ref [140], ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Swarm Control, Planning, and Autonomy
subsections.content:
Task allocation in MAV swarms links high-level mission objectives to local action selection under communication, energy, and sensing constraints. Early market-based approaches remain influential because they convert heterogeneous capabilities and dynamic costs into distributed bidding rules with modest coordination overhead; representative formulations include auction-based multirobot coordination and role allocation mechanisms that explicitly address uncertainty and limited communication ref [142], ref [143]. For aerial teams, these ideas are often combined with consensus and distributed optimization so that assignment decisions can be revised online as vehicles fail, targets move, or information value changes ref [144], ref [145].

Beyond one-shot assignment, cooperative decision-making increasingly treats the swarm as an information-seeking collective. Submodular task allocation provides provable near-optimality for sensing and coverage objectives under decentralization assumptions ref [146], while decentralized data fusion and active perception frameworks couple who-goes-where decisions with what-to-measure decisions ref [147]. Such formulations are particularly relevant to MAVs, where limited endurance makes value-of-information and path cost tightly coupled. Multi-UAV mission planning has therefore moved toward receding-horizon and mixed-integer formulations that jointly schedule tasks, trajectories, and timing constraints ref [148], ref [149].

A complementary line of work emphasizes robustness and scalability through biologically inspired collective choice. Response-threshold and swarm-intelligence mechanisms enable adaptive division of labor without centralized bookkeeping, especially in environments with intermittent communication or unknown task arrival rates ref [150]. More recently, decentralized partially observable decision processes and learned policies have been explored to capture cooperative uncertainty, but their practical deployment still depends on maintaining tractable communication and safety guarantees. Overall, effective task allocation in MAV swarms requires balancing computational tractability, assignment optimality, and resilience to real-time disturbances.

subsections.section_title: Swarm Control, Planning, and Autonomy
subsections.subsection_title: Adaptive, Learning-Based, and Bio-Inspired Swarm Strategies
subsections.content:
Adaptive and learning-based swarm strategies seek to preserve the scalability of decentralized control while improving robustness to model uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, and changing mission objectives. A central theme is replacing hand-crafted interaction rules with policies learned from data or experience, often by embedding communication and coordination directly into the policy architecture. Early work on multi-agent reinforcement learning highlighted the non-stationarity and scalability challenges of decentralized learning in cooperative settings ref [151], while later actor-critic formulations with centralized training and decentralized execution improved policy learning for partially observable teams ref [152]. For swarm-scale coordination, graph-based policy models have become particularly influential because they encode local interactions and permutation invariance, enabling transfer across team sizes and communication topologies ref [153], ref [154].

For MAV swarms, these ideas are often paired with bio-inspired principles such as flocking, stigmergy, and collective gradient following. Olfati-Saber’s theoretical treatment of flocking remains foundational for designing local interaction laws that yield coherent global motion ref [11], and Reynolds’ classic behavioral model continues to inform rule-based cohesion, separation, and alignment mechanisms ref [3]. More recent work has shown that learned communication can outperform fixed protocols in cooperative decision-making ref [155], while graph neural networks have been used to learn decentralized controllers that generalize over robot teams and tasks ref [156]. Such methods are attractive for adaptive formation reshaping, exploration, and target tracking when communication is sparse or intermittent.

Despite their promise, learning-based swarm controllers still face important barriers to deployment, including sample inefficiency, verification difficulty, and brittleness under distribution shift. Surveys of deep reinforcement learning for multi-robot systems emphasize the need to integrate formal safety filters, domain randomization, and sim-to-real transfer techniques before these methods can be trusted in safety-critical aerial missions ref [157], ref [158]. Consequently, a practical direction is hybrid autonomy, in which biologically inspired local rules or model-based safety layers provide certifiable structure, while learned components adapt task-level behavior online.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Challenges in Real-World Deployment
subsections.subsection_title: Scalability From Small Teams to Large Swarms
subsections.content:
Scalability is a central obstacle in moving MAV swarms from small, tightly coordinated teams to large collectives. Architectures that rely on centralized planning or all-to-all communication often exhibit computation, bandwidth, and latency growth that becomes prohibitive as swarm size increases. Early formation-control and consensus studies already emphasized that stability and convergence depend strongly on graph structure and local interaction rules rather than global coordination, motivating distributed designs whose complexity scales with neighborhood size rather than fleet size [1], ref [11], ref [26].

Even with distributed control, scaling remains constrained by coupling between communication, estimation, and collision avoidance. Large teams must maintain safe separation under intermittent links, packet loss, and asynchronous updates, conditions under which nominally elegant flocking laws can degrade or fragment [4], ref [160]. Practical demonstrations of decentralized multi-UAV systems and swarm flight have shown that local sensing, relative localization, and behavior-based coordination can reduce dependence on infrastructure, but they also reveal bottlenecks in shared wireless channels, limited onboard compute, and sensitivity to topology changes [6], ref [162], ref [163].

Consequently, scalability is not merely a matter of adding more vehicles; it requires co-design across algorithms, communication protocols, and system architecture. Bio-inspired swarm frameworks offer robustness through simple local rules, while recent surveys on UAV swarms note that verification, predictable performance bounds, and scalable task allocation remain open for field deployment at large population sizes [9], ref [165].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Challenges in Real-World Deployment
subsections.content:
Robustness in MAV swarms must be understood as resilience to both internal failures and exogenous uncertainty. In practice, fielded systems face intermittent communication, packet loss, sensing degradation, actuator faults, and large model mismatch induced by wind and payload variation. Early decentralized flocking and consensus formulations already highlighted that stability and cohesion depend critically on local-information consistency and graph connectivity rather than centralized supervision, making them attractive under communication uncertainty but also exposing fragility to topology changes and delays ref [11], ref [5]. Subsequent work on cooperative control under switching interaction graphs formalized conditions under which agreement can still be preserved despite link failures and time-varying neighborhoods ref [166].

At the vehicle level, robust deployment requires estimation and control architectures that tolerate sensor dropout and aggressive disturbances. Practical quadrotor systems have demonstrated recovery through onboard visual-inertial state estimation and aerodynamic disturbance rejection, reducing dependence on any single sensing modality ref [167], ref [52]. For multi-robot operation, distributed model predictive control and related optimization-based schemes improve constraint handling and collision avoidance, but their real-world robustness is often limited by latency, inaccurate models, and infeasible optimization under failures ref [168]. Fault-tolerant formation and containment controllers explicitly address partial actuator or agent loss, showing that degraded but safe collective behavior can be maintained when redundancy is built into local control laws ref [169], ref [170].

More broadly, resilience at swarm scale is increasingly treated as a system property that combines graceful degradation, online reconfiguration, and formal safety guarantees. Barrier-certificate methods and safety filters can maintain collision avoidance under uncertain neighbor behavior, while resilient distributed estimation and consensus seek to isolate malfunctioning or adversarial agents ref [171], ref [172]. The remaining challenge is to integrate these guarantees with realistic onboard computation, asynchronous networks, and heterogeneous failure modes typical of long-duration outdoor missions.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Challenges in Real-World Deployment
subsections.subsection_title: Operation in GPS-Denied and Cluttered Environments
subsections.content:
Operation in GPS-denied and cluttered environments exposes a central gap between laboratory swarm demonstrations and field deployment: global positioning, persistent communication, and obstacle-free airspace cannot be assumed. For individual MAVs, this has driven a shift toward onboard state estimation based on visual-inertial sensing and lidar, including tightly coupled visual-inertial odometry and lidar-inertial odometry that remain accurate during aggressive motion and in partially structured scenes ref [60], ref [173], ref [174]. However, swarm settings compound the problem because estimator drift, intermittent observability, and sensing occlusions propagate into coordination errors, especially when vehicles must maintain formations or deconflict in narrow spaces.

Recent work therefore emphasizes fully autonomous navigation stacks that jointly solve localization, mapping, planning, and control onboard. Systems such as local replanning with motion primitives or incremental trajectory optimization have enabled quadrotors to fly safely through dense clutter using only onboard perception ref [175], ref [176]. At the swarm level, decentralized collision avoidance and reciprocal avoidance methods provide scalable deconfliction without centralized motion planning, but their assumptions on relative state accuracy and communication reliability are harder to satisfy indoors, in forests, or around infrastructure ref [133], ref [177]. Multi-robot mapping and relative localization can reduce dependence on external infrastructure, yet they introduce synchronization, data association, and inter-robot consistency challenges that remain unresolved at larger swarm sizes ref [178], ref [179].

A recurring deployment lesson is that perception failures dominate before control limits do. Illumination changes, textureless surfaces, dust, foliage, and dynamic obstacles degrade camera-based pipelines, while lidar payload and power costs constrain small MAVs. Learning-based depth prediction and perception-aware planning offer partial mitigation, but robustness certification remains limited ref [180]. Consequently, reliable swarm operation in cluttered GPS-denied environments still depends on careful sensor redundancy, conservative planning margins, and graceful degradation strategies rather than purely nominal autonomy.

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Challenges in Real-World Deployment
subsections.content:
Energy endurance remains a primary bottleneck in deploying MAV swarms outside controlled demonstrations. Limited battery capacity constrains flight time, payload, onboard computation, and communication, creating strong coupling between vehicle design and mission planning. Reviews of multirotor energy use consistently show that endurance is highly sensitive to mass, aerodynamic efficiency, and aggressive maneuvering, while practical field operations add further losses from sensing, processing, and safety margins ref [181], ref [182]. For swarms, these limits compound at the system level: short individual sorties force frequent task reallocation, reduce persistent coverage, and increase the probability that a mission fails because a subset of vehicles must return early or reserve energy for contingencies.

Mission sustainability therefore depends on energy-aware coordination rather than vehicle-level optimization alone. Recent work has formulated informative path planning and coverage under explicit battery constraints, showing that routes, sensing actions, and return-to-base decisions must be co-optimized to preserve team-level utility ref [183], ref [184]. Charging and replenishment infrastructure is equally critical. Autonomous battery swapping and docking stations can reduce human intervention and enable cyclic operation, but introduce queueing, localization, and scheduling problems that become harder with swarm size ref [185], ref [186]. Wireless charging and contact-based recharging have also been explored for aerial robots, although transfer efficiency, docking precision, and weather robustness remain limiting factors ref [187].

A further challenge is that endurance prediction in real deployments is uncertain. Wind, temperature, payload variation, and battery aging can invalidate nominal energy models, motivating adaptive estimation and receding-horizon planning that update feasible mission duration online ref [188], ref [189]. More broadly, sustainable swarm operation will likely require joint advances in lightweight airframe design, energy-aware autonomy, and infrastructure-assisted persistence, including long-duration concepts such as solar-powered UAVs for specific operating envelopes ref [190].

subsections.section_title: Fundamental Challenges in Real-World Deployment
subsections.content:
Human–swarm interaction is a central deployment bottleneck because a single operator cannot issue low-level commands to many MAVs while also maintaining situation awareness. The literature therefore emphasizes supervisory control, in which humans specify intent, priorities, or spatial goals while autonomy allocates tasks and resolves local coordination. Early analyses of neglect tolerance and fan-out showed that effective multi-robot supervision depends as much on interface design and autonomy allocation as on platform capability itself [1], while mixed-initiative control frameworks argued for dynamically shifting authority between human and automation to manage workload and uncertainty [2].

For MAV swarms, the main challenge is to expose collective behavior through abstractions that remain interpretable under communication delays, partial observability, and rapidly changing environments. Studies of human interaction with robot swarms have highlighted the value of global commands, environment-oriented control, and visual analytics over individual vehicle teleoperation [3], and broader surveys have converged on scalable interaction modalities such as gesture, sketch, language, and shared-autonomy interfaces [4]. Formal work on flexible human-swarm interaction further stresses that control inputs should map to swarm-level primitives such as coverage, formation bias, or target assignment rather than robot-specific actions [5].

A second deployment issue is trust calibration and explainability: operators must understand why the swarm is reconfiguring, failing, or rejecting commands. Human factors studies in multi-robot systems show that transparency and adaptive autonomy strongly influence workload, intervention frequency, and mission effectiveness [6]. In parallel, recent work on intent interfaces and augmented-reality interaction for drone teams suggests that immersive spatial interfaces can reduce command ambiguity and improve shared situational awareness in cluttered settings [7,8]. Looking ahead, robust supervisory control for fielded MAV swarms will require principled levels of autonomy, resilient communication-aware interfaces, and evaluation methods that jointly measure operator cognition, swarm performance, and safety under realistic mission tempo [4,6,9].

subsections.section_title: Evaluation Methodologies, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation, Digital Twins, and Experimental Testbeds
subsections.content:
Simulation remains the dominant entry point for MAV-swarm research because it permits rapid iteration over coordination, estimation, and control under controllable disturbances, scalable team sizes, and repeatable initial conditions. In practice, the field has relied heavily on robotics simulators that expose realistic rigid-body dynamics, sensing, and middleware integration, including Gazebo ref [200], AirSim ref [201], Flightmare ref [202], and RotorS ref [73]. These platforms lower the cost of developing distributed perception and planning stacks before flight, but their simplifying assumptions still create a persistent sim-to-real gap in aerodynamics, wireless communication, state-estimation drift, and inter-robot interference.

Recent work increasingly treats simulation not only as a design tool but as part of a digital-twin workflow, where online state synchronization and higher-fidelity environment models support diagnosis, predictive safety analysis, and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation. Although fully mature digital twins for MAV swarms remain uncommon, adjacent developments in high-fidelity photorealistic and physically grounded simulation, such as CARLA ref [203] and the Unreal Engine–based AirSim ecosystem ref [201], point toward continuously updated virtual counterparts that can support scenario replay, fault injection, and operator training. For learning-based swarm policies, simulation is especially important because domain randomization and massively parallel rollouts can reduce transfer brittleness and expose rare corner cases before deployment ref [204].

Experimental testbeds are nevertheless indispensable, since many collective-flight failure modes only emerge with real vehicles. Motion-capture laboratories and outdoor multi-UAV platforms have enabled reproducible demonstrations of formation flight, cooperative transport, and agile multi-robot coordination ref [126], ref [205], while standardized open-source platforms such as Crazyswarm have substantially improved accessibility and repeatability for large numbers of nano-quadrotors ref [8]. Looking forward, the strongest validation pipelines will couple simulator benchmarks, digital-twin monitoring, and staged hardware experiments, with explicit reporting of fidelity limits, calibration procedures, and transfer performance across environments ref [202], ref [73], ref [8], ref [206].

subsections.section_title: Evaluation Methodologies, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Benchmarking in MAV swarms remains fragmented because studies often optimize different objectives—coverage, throughput, latency, energy, robustness, or safety—under incomparable assumptions. A useful benchmark should therefore report both task-level performance and system-level properties such as scalability with swarm size, resilience to communication loss, and sensitivity to sensing uncertainty. This lesson is visible across canonical swarm tasks including aggregation, dispersion, and flocking, where apparently similar controllers can differ markedly once communication range, packet delay, or obstacle density are varied ref [207], ref [11]. In coverage and exploration settings, metrics such as mapped area per unit time, overlap, and localization drift are especially important because they expose trade-offs hidden by single-score summaries ref [208], ref [27].

Reproducibility further depends on standardized experimental protocols. In robotics more broadly, community efforts have emphasized repeatable benchmarking, clear dataset and code release, and explicit reporting of hardware, software, and statistical procedures ref [209], ref [210]. For aerial systems, this implies documenting flight arena dimensions, motion-capture availability, estimator configuration, radio stack, onboard compute, and failure handling, since these factors strongly affect observed swarm behavior. Competition-style evaluations and common simulation platforms have helped establish shared tasks and metrics for multi-robot coordination, but transferability from simulation to physical MAV swarms remains a persistent concern ref [211], ref [212].

A practical direction is to pair benchmark suites with open logs, seeded scenarios, and confidence intervals over repeated trials rather than best-case demonstrations. Recent benchmarking discussions in autonomous-robotics and multi-agent learning also highlight the need to evaluate generalization, not merely nominal performance, by varying environments, disturbances, and team composition ref [210], ref [213]. For MAV swarms, rigorous reproducibility will likely require integrated benchmarks spanning simulation, hardware-in-the-loop, and real-flight experiments, together with versioned artifacts and negative-result reporting ref [212], ref [214].

subsections.section_title: Evaluation Methodologies, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Verification and validation (V&V) for MAV swarms must address both low-level flight safety and emergent multi-agent behavior. At the controller level, formal analysis has been used to certify stability and collision-avoidance properties for quadrotor systems, while reachable-set methods provide conservative guarantees under bounded disturbances and model uncertainty ref [215], ref [216]. For decentralized swarms, safety assurance is harder because guarantees must compose across many interacting vehicles; control barrier functions and related safety filters have therefore become attractive as minimally invasive runtime mechanisms that enforce pairwise separation and safe set invariance even when higher-level planners are learned or heuristic ref [135], ref [217].

Validation, however, cannot rely on formal proofs alone because swarm performance depends strongly on sensing imperfections, communication loss, and environment complexity. Hardware-in-the-loop and staged field testing remain essential, especially for stress-testing perception and coordination stacks under realistic latency and packet-drop conditions. Runtime assurance architectures, in which an advanced controller is monitored by a verified backup policy, offer a practical bridge between formal guarantees and deployable autonomy ref [218]. This perspective aligns with broader safety cases for learning-enabled autonomous systems, which emphasize evidence integration across simulation, testing, and formal methods rather than any single technique ref [219].

A key open issue is scalable assurance for adaptive and learning-based swarms. Neural-network verification has advanced for perception and control components, but current tools remain limited in dimensionality and are difficult to lift to closed-loop, many-agent settings ref [220], ref [221]. Similarly, formal falsification and stress testing can reveal corner cases in autonomous systems, yet constructing representative adversarial scenarios for cooperative aerial swarms remains largely unresolved ref [222]. Future safety assurance will likely combine compositional verification, online monitors, and statistically rigorous campaign testing to support certification-ready evidence for collective flight.

subsections.section_title: Evaluation Methodologies, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Security in MAV swarms is fundamentally cross-layer: compromise can arise through wireless links, distributed coordination logic, localization pipelines, and the cyber-physical interface itself. Early analyses of unmanned aerial vehicle security emphasized the fragility of command-and-control channels, GPS dependence, and onboard software attack surfaces, while later work on cyber-physical security of networked robotic systems highlighted how estimation, communication, and control vulnerabilities can cascade into unsafe collective behavior ref [223], ref [224]. For swarms, these risks are amplified by inter-agent trust and tight coupling, so local compromise may propagate into formation breakup, mission deviation, or collision.

A major threat class is adversarial manipulation of sensing and navigation. GPS spoofing against civilian UAVs has been demonstrated in practice, showing that attackers can induce trajectory hijacking without obvious alarms ref [225]. Vision-based autonomy is likewise vulnerable: physically realizable perturbations can mislead deep perception stacks used by robots and autonomous vehicles, raising concerns for collaborative obstacle avoidance and target tracking ref [226], ref [227]. Communication-layer attacks such as jamming, packet dropping, and false-data injection are also especially damaging in consensus-based or leader-follower swarms, where stability often depends on timely and trustworthy neighbor information ref [224], ref [228].

Privacy is an adjacent concern because MAV swarms increasingly perform persistent sensing over populated areas. Beyond protecting telemetry and video streams, privacy-preserving operation may require data minimization, secure multi-party coordination, and accountable access control for edge/cloud offloading. Recent surveys on drone cybersecurity and UAV intrusion detection argue for defense-in-depth combining secure communication, anomaly detection, resilient state estimation, and formal runtime assurance ref [229], ref [230]. Open problems include scalable trust management under intermittent connectivity, coordinated response to compromised agents, and benchmark suites that evaluate both mission performance and adversarial robustness in swarm settings ref [229], ref [231].

subsections.section_title: Evaluation Methodologies, Safety, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Open Problems and Emerging Research Directions
subsections.content:
A central open problem is closing the sim-to-real gap for large MAV swarms under coupled aerodynamic, sensing, and communication effects. Existing robot learning and control pipelines remain brittle when policies trained in simulation encounter unmodeled disturbances, latency, and inter-robot downwash. Domain randomization has improved transfer in robotics, but its assumptions are often weak for safety-critical aerial collectives ref [204]. Richer digital twins, online system identification, and uncertainty-aware adaptation therefore remain important directions, especially when scaling from tens to hundreds of vehicles.

Another emerging direction is toward certifiable, resilient autonomy that unifies planning, learning, and formal safety constraints. Safe multi-agent coordination is still dominated by simplified dynamics or pairwise avoidance assumptions, while dense swarms require compositional guarantees under packet loss, partial observability, and changing team membership. Control barrier functions offer a promising route to runtime safety filtering ref [135], and scalable formal methods for large networked robot teams are beginning to appear ref [232]. At the same time, learning-enabled components raise unresolved questions about specification, verification, and assurance in autonomous systems ref [233].

More broadly, the field needs benchmarks that reward mission-level robustness, energy efficiency, and graceful degradation rather than only nominal formation accuracy. Emerging application domains such as autonomous drone racing have catalyzed progress in agile perception and planning ref [234], while vision-based swarm demonstrations highlight the potential of end-to-end onboard autonomy ref [235]. Future work should also address self-organized scalability inspired by swarm intelligence ref [7], human-swarm supervision for real deployments ref [236], and security against adversarial perception and communication attacks on learning-based UAV systems ref [237].
